blocks.text: Imagine sending a letter across the world. How does it find its way through countless postal systems? In computer networks, the Internet Protocol (IP) plays a similar role for data packets.

blocks.markdown: The Internet Protocol (IP) is a fundamental component of the network layer, responsible for delivering packets from the source host to the destination host across multiple networks. In this lesson, we will explore the structure of IP datagrams, the role of the Time-to-Live (TTL) field, and supporting protocols like ICMP and ARP.

blocks.title: IP Datagram
blocks.text: An IP datagram is a basic unit of data transfer in the Internet Protocol, consisting of a header and payload. The header contains essential information for routing and delivery.

blocks.markdown: One critical field in the IP header is the Time-to-Live (TTL) field. The TTL field is an 8-bit value that specifies the maximum number of hops a packet can take before being discarded. Each router that forwards the packet decreases the TTL by one. If the TTL reaches zero, the packet is dropped, preventing it from circulating indefinitely.

blocks.title: Purpose of TTL
blocks.text: The TTL field prevents packets from looping indefinitely in the network by limiting the number of hops they can take.

blocks.title: Calculating TTL Effect
blocks.prompt: Suppose a packet starts with a TTL of 5 and traverses 3 routers. What will the TTL be after these hops?

steps.text: Start with an initial TTL of 5.

blocks.answer: The TTL will be 2 after traversing 3 routers.

blocks.markdown: The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) is used to map an IP address to a physical machine address (MAC address) in a local network. When a device wants to communicate with another device on the same network, it sends an ARP request to find the MAC address corresponding to the target IP address.

blocks.title: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)
blocks.text: ARP is a protocol used to map an IP address to a MAC address within a local network.

blocks.title: ARP Request Process
blocks.prompt: Describe the process of an ARP request when a device wants to communicate with another device on the same network.

steps.text: The device broadcasts an ARP request packet to all devices on the local network, asking for the MAC address of the target IP address.
The device with the matching IP address responds with an ARP reply, providing its MAC address.

blocks.answer: The ARP request process involves broadcasting a request for the MAC address associated with a specific IP address, and receiving a reply with the MAC address.

blocks.markdown: ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) is used for network diagnostics and error reporting. Two common tools that use ICMP are **ping** and **traceroute**. Ping tests connectivity by sending ICMP Echo Request messages and waiting for Echo Reply messages. Traceroute maps the path packets take to a destination by sending packets with incrementally increasing TTL values.

blocks.title: Ping and Traceroute
blocks.text: Ping checks connectivity, while traceroute finds the path packets take to a destination.

points: The TTL field in IP datagrams prevents routing loops by limiting the number of hops.
ARP resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses within a local network.
Ping and traceroute use ICMP for network diagnostics and path mapping.
